analytics.title: Analytics
analytics.nobodyOnSite: Nobody on the site in the last 5 minutes

help.title: Help
help.subtitle: What each part of this page does.

analytics.audienceBlurb: The headline tiles — how many people came, how much they looked at, and how many are here right now.
analytics.audienceVisitorsD: Distinct people in the selected period. A visitor is a privacy-friendly daily hash of IP and browser — no cookies — so the same person on two days counts twice.
analytics.audiencePageviewsD: Every page load, including SPA route changes. One visitor can rack up many pageviews, so this is always higher than visitors.
analytics.audienceSessionsD: A visit — one or more pageviews with no 30-minute gap. A returning visitor later in the day starts a fresh session.
analytics.audienceLiveD: Distinct visitors active in the last five minutes, updated as the page refreshes. The 'Right now' panel lists the pages they're on.
analytics.behaviorBlurb: How engaged visits are, and what people do once they arrive — the Pages, Engagement and Clicks tabs.
analytics.behaviorBounceD: Share of sessions that left after a single pageview without interacting. Lower is usually better — the delta arrow is coloured accordingly.
analytics.behaviorAvgSessionD: Average visible time across a whole visit. A backgrounded tab doesn't count, so this is real attention time, not just tab-open time.
analytics.behaviorTimePageT: Avg. time on page / Pages per session
analytics.behaviorTimePageD: How long a single page holds attention, and how many pages a typical visit touches. Higher pages-per-session means people explore more.
analytics.behaviorPagesD: Your most-viewed pages, plus where visits begin (entry) and where they end (exit). Click a row to filter every number to that page.
analytics.behaviorEngagementD: Scroll depth and landing performance, a traffic heatmap by hour and weekday, and which CTAs get clicked and where on the page.
analytics.acquisitionBlurb: Where visitors come from — the Sources, Geography and Technology tabs.
analytics.acquisitionChannelsD: Channels group traffic into Direct, Organic, Social and Paid; Referrers name the exact sites sending it. Click a referrer to filter by it.
analytics.acquisitionUtmD: Traffic tagged with campaign parameters, so you can measure a specific push separately from everything else.
analytics.acquisitionGeoD: A world map shaded by volume, plus ranked countries and browser languages — useful for deciding what to translate.
analytics.acquisitionTechD: Browsers, operating systems, devices and screen sizes. A surprise here — lots of an old browser, say — can explain layout complaints.
analytics.conversionBlurb: Whether visits turn into the outcomes you care about — the Goals, Events, Funnel, Retention and Errors tabs.
analytics.conversionGoalsD: Completion rates for the actions you've defined as goals — the share of visitors doing the thing that matters.
analytics.conversionEventsD: Custom events fired via rta.track(), with their totals and any revenue value summed across them.
analytics.conversionFunnelD: A step-by-step path you define. Each step shows how many sessions reached it and where people drop off.
analytics.conversionRetentionD: Weekly cohorts and how many visitors come back over the following weeks — a read on whether the product holds people.
analytics.conversionErrorsD: Client-side errors the tracker forwarded, so a broken page shows up here rather than only in complaints.

reports.title: Reports help
reports.schedulesBlurb: A report is a saved schedule: which sites, how often, and who it goes to. It keeps sending until you pause or delete it.
reports.schedulesActiveD: How many schedules are currently sending. Pausing a report keeps its configuration and recipients — it simply stops delivering until you switch it back on.
reports.schedulesNextD: When the soonest report goes out, and which one it is. Sends are queued in the workspace's timezone, so a change to the schedule takes effect from the next run onward.
reports.schedulesFrequencyD: Daily, weekly or monthly. The period covered always matches the frequency, and each email compares it against the previous period of the same length.
reports.schedulesSitesD: A report can cover one site or several. With more than one, the email carries a section per site rather than blending their numbers together.
reports.recipientsBlurb: Reports usually go to people outside the account — a client, a manager — so addresses are listed in full rather than counted.
reports.recipientsReachD: Unique addresses across all active reports. Someone on two reports counts once here but still receives both emails.
reports.recipientsNoAccountD: Recipients don't sign up for anything. They receive the email and can act on it without ever opening the dashboard.
reports.recipientsUnsubD: Anyone who opts out stays visible on the card, greyed out, instead of quietly disappearing — so a report that looks like it's reaching five people isn't silently reaching three.
reports.recipientsTestD: Sends the report exactly as scheduled, immediately, to you only. Use it to check the content before real recipients ever see it.
reports.contentsBlurb: Headline numbers in the body, the full breakdown attached, and optionally a link to the live dashboard.
reports.contentsSummaryD: Visitors, pageviews, sessions and SEO score for the period, each with its change against the previous one.
reports.contentsSheetD: Every breakdown — pages, sources, geography, devices — on its own sheet, so a recipient can pivot the raw numbers themselves.
reports.contentsLiveLinkD: Optional. Including it publishes the workspace's public dashboard: anyone holding the link can open it, forwarded email included. Leave it off if the recipient list isn't trusted.
reports.deliveryBlurb: How the mail actually leaves, and what to check when it doesn't arrive.
reports.deliveryNotConfiguredD: When this deployment has no mail credentials, schedules still save but nothing is delivered. They begin sending as soon as mail is configured — no need to recreate them.
reports.deliveryWhatsAppD: Available on plans that include it. It sends a short summary to the owner's verified mobile number alongside the email, not instead of it.
reports.deliverySpamD: First delivery to a new domain often lands in spam. Ask recipients to mark it as not-spam once; later sends then arrive normally.

billing.title: Billing help
billing.usageBlurb: What you're on now, how much of this cycle's quota is left, and when it resets.
billing.usageCycleD: The billing period your plan runs on — monthly or yearly. Quotas are monthly either way; a yearly plan is a discount on price, not a bigger single pool.
billing.usageUsedD: How much of this month's quota you've spent. Both reset at the start of each monthly period, whatever your billing cycle.
billing.usageExpiredD: The period ended without renewal. Existing data stays readable, but new audits and crawls are paused until you renew.
billing.usageRenewalD: When the next period begins and quotas reset. Purchases don't auto-renew — a plan is a one-time charge for one month or one year.
billing.plansBlurb: The plan grid. Each card lists its monthly audit and crawl quota alongside the features it unlocks.
billing.plansCurrentD: The plan backing your account right now. Its card is marked rather than buyable, and a lower tier is shown as a downgrade.
billing.plansUpgradeD: Takes effect immediately. The new quota is available as soon as payment clears, without waiting for the current period to end.
billing.plansCyclesD: The toggle above the grid reprices every card. Yearly is charged once for twelve months at a lower effective rate.
billing.plansCurrencyD: Prices display in your local currency where supported. The charge itself is made in the currency shown at checkout.
billing.addonsBlurb: Extra audits or crawls for when you outgrow the monthly quota without wanting a bigger plan.
billing.addonsNoExpiryD: Unlike plan quota, bought credits carry across periods. They sit alongside the plan allowance rather than replacing it.
billing.addonsPlanFirstD: Credits are only drawn on once the month's plan allowance is exhausted, so nothing bought is wasted at a reset.
billing.addonsBalanceD: The counters separate “from plan” and “bought” deliberately — they behave differently at the end of a period, and a single total would hide that.
billing.historyBlurb: Every charge on the account, newest first, with an invoice for each.
billing.historyInvoiceD: A downloadable record of one payment — plan or add-on — with the amount, currency, date and payment reference.
billing.historyFailedD: A failed charge is listed too, so an unexpectedly unchanged plan has a visible explanation rather than none.
billing.historyRefundD: Refunds appear as their own entry against the original charge rather than removing it, keeping the history an accurate ledger.

developers.title: Developers help
developers.keysBlurb: Server-side secrets scoped to this workspace. They authenticate the Platform API — creating projects and sites for your own users from your backend.
developers.keysScopeD: A key only reaches the workspace it was created in. Switching workspace in the rail shows that workspace's keys, not a global list.
developers.keysNameD: A label so you can tell keys apart — “Production backend”, “Staging”. Only you see it; it carries no permissions of its own.
developers.keysPrefixD: The visible first characters of a key, shown in the list. Enough to match a key against your environment variables without revealing the secret.
developers.keysLastUsedD: When the key last authenticated a request. “Never used” on a key you deployed days ago usually means the integration isn't sending it.
developers.securityBlurb: A key is a password for your workspace's data. Treat it like one.
developers.securityOnceD: The full secret appears only in the dialog that creates it. Only a hash is stored, so it genuinely cannot be recovered later — copy it before closing.
developers.securityServerOnlyD: Never put a key in browser code, a mobile app, or a public repository. Anything shipped to a client is readable by anyone who receives it. Use an environment variable on your server.
developers.securityRevokeD: Revocation is immediate and permanent. Any integration still sending the key starts receiving 401 Unauthorized, so roll a replacement in first if the caller must stay up.
developers.securityLeakD: Revoke it and create a new one. There is no way to restrict a leaked key to fewer permissions — replacement is the only fix.
developers.docsBlurb: The tracking snippet, custom events and the full Platform API reference live on the docs site.
developers.docsInstallD: The one-line snippet that starts collecting pageviews, plus framework notes for single-page apps where route changes need to be reported explicitly.
developers.docsEventsD: rta.track() sends your own named events, optionally with a revenue value, which then appear on the Analytics page's Events and Goals tabs.
developers.docsApiD: The endpoints an API key unlocks — creating workspaces and sites, and reading stats — for embedding analytics in your own product.

share.title: Public dashboard help
share.linkBlurb: One read-only link to this workspace's dashboard. Anyone holding it can open it — there is no sign-in and no per-person access.
share.linkToggleD: Off means the link returns nothing. Switching it on publishes immediately, so treat turning it on as the moment the data becomes public.
share.linkCredentialD: Whoever has the URL has access, including anyone it gets forwarded to. Share it the way you'd share a password.
share.linkReplaceD: Generates a fresh URL and permanently breaks the old one. This is how you revoke access from someone who already has the link.
share.linkLiveD: A public dashboard reflects the same numbers you see, updating as they do. It is not a frozen snapshot of the moment you shared it.
share.visibleBlurb: Panel by panel control over the public view, so a client sees traffic without seeing everything.
share.visiblePanelsD: Each panel — headline metrics, pages, sources, geography, technology — is individually switchable. A panel that's off is absent from the public page, not blurred out.
share.visibleActivityD: The live “right now” view. Useful for showing a launch in progress; switch it off if you'd rather not expose current traffic in real time.
share.visibleScopeD: The public dashboard covers this workspace. To share a subset, put those sites in a workspace of their own and share that one.
share.seoBlurb: SEO audits share separately from the analytics dashboard — each audited page gets its own read-only link.
share.seoPerAuditD: Turning on sharing for one audit doesn't affect any other, and doesn't publish the analytics dashboard.
share.seoShowsD: The score, the issues found, and the recommendations — the same report you see, minus anything you switch off for it.
share.seoOffD: Disabling a shared audit takes its link out of service straight away. Anyone with the URL gets nothing from that point on.
share.neverBlurb: Some things are excluded from every public view regardless of the switches above.
share.neverBillingD: Your email, plan, invoices and payment history are never part of a shared page.
share.neverKeysD: API keys, workspace settings and site configuration are never exposed. A public viewer cannot change anything.
share.neverOtherD: A link reaches exactly one workspace. It reveals no evidence that any other exists.

workspaces.title: Workspaces help
workspaces.workspacesBlurb: A workspace groups the sites you want to look at together. The rail's switcher decides which one every other page is showing.
workspaces.workspacesGroupingD: One client, one product, one environment — whatever you'd want to see totalled on a single dashboard. Sites in different workspaces are never summed.
workspaces.workspacesActiveD: Analytics, SEO, Reports and Developers all read from the workspace selected in the rail. Switching it reloads every panel against the other dataset.
workspaces.workspacesRenameD: The name is a label only. Renaming affects nothing else — no link breaks, no data moves.
workspaces.workspacesDeleteD: Permanently removes the workspace and everything in it: sites, collected events, API keys and any public link. This cannot be undone.
workspaces.sitesBlurb: A site is one domain being tracked. It's what the tracking snippet reports against.
workspaces.sitesDomainD: Events are accepted for the domain you register. A mismatch between the site here and where the snippet actually runs is the usual reason a new install shows nothing.
workspaces.sitesSiteIdD: The identifier baked into the tracking snippet. Each site has its own, which is what keeps two sites in one workspace separate.
workspaces.sitesWaitingD: A site shows no numbers until its first event arrives. Load a page with the snippet installed and it appears within seconds.
workspaces.sitesRemoveD: Deletes the site and its collected events from the workspace. The snippet keeps firing until you also remove it from the page, but the events are discarded.
workspaces.installBlurb: Tracking starts when the snippet runs on the page. The full guide lives in the docs.
workspaces.installWhereD: In the page head, on every page you want counted. A snippet only on the homepage measures only the homepage.
workspaces.installSpaD: Client-side route changes aren't page loads. The docs cover reporting them so an SPA doesn't record one pageview per visit.
workspaces.installBlockersD: Some blockers drop third-party analytics. A visit you make yourself not appearing doesn't mean the install is broken — check from another browser before debugging.

seo.title: SEO report help
seo.overviewBlurb: The at-a-glance verdict on this page: one headline score, how it breaks down, and what to fix first. Start here, then open a tab for the detail.
seo.overviewScoreD: A 0-100 roll-up of every check in the audit. 90+ is good, 50-89 needs work, under 50 is poor — the same bands Google's PageSpeed uses.
seo.overviewCategoriesD: SEO, Performance, Accessibility and Best practices, each scored on its own. A low category tells you which tab to open next.
seo.overviewSeverityD: Critical issues actively hurt ranking or block crawling — fix those first. Warnings are worth doing; suggestions are polish.
seo.overviewClusterD: Which part of the page the problems concentrate in, so you know whether it's a meta, content, technical or links job.
seo.overviewTrendD: How the overall score moved across your recent audits of this URL. A fix that worked shows up as a step up here.
seo.metaBlurb: The tags in the page's <head> that search engines and social platforms read — title, description, canonical, and the Open Graph / Twitter tags that control how a shared link looks.
seo.metaPreviewD: Roughly how the page renders on a results page. Seeing the title and description truncate is more useful than a raw character count.
seo.metaTitleD: Aim for 30-60 characters. Too long and it's cut off in results; too short and you're wasting the strongest on-page ranking signal.
seo.metaDescriptionD: 120-160 characters. It doesn't rank the page but it's the sales pitch under the title — a good one lifts click-through.
seo.metaCanonicalD: Tells search engines which URL is the 'real' one when the same content is reachable at several addresses, so ranking signals don't get split.
seo.metaSocialD: Open Graph and Twitter Card tags decide the image, title and text shown when the page is shared. Missing ones mean an ugly or blank card.
seo.contentBlurb: How the page's actual copy stacks up: length, heading structure, images, links and readability — the raw material search engines and readers judge.
seo.contentWordsD: 300+ is a reasonable floor for a page meant to rank. Thin pages struggle to demonstrate relevance for anything competitive.
seo.contentH1D: Exactly one H1 per page — it's the page's main title for crawlers. Zero or several muddies what the page is about.
seo.contentReadabilityD: Flesch Reading Ease, 0-100. Higher is easier to read. Very low scores mean dense sentences most visitors will bounce off.
seo.contentQualityD: A composite of length, headings, alt text, links and structured data — a single number for how complete the page's on-page basics are.
seo.contentKeywordsD: The words that make up the most of the body text. Useful for a sanity check that the page is actually about what you think it is.
seo.technicalBlurb: The under-the-hood signals a crawler looks for on every page, plus the server response and the lab Core Web Vitals from Lighthouse.
seo.technicalChecksD: Pass/fail signals: HTTPS, a mobile viewport tag, Open Graph, structured data and image alt text. Fails here are usually quick wins.
seo.technicalResponseD: The HTTP status, response time and page size the server returned. A slow or oversized response drags performance down everywhere.
seo.technicalCrawlerFilesD: robots.txt and the sitemap — how search engines discover the rest of the site. A blocked or missing one can hide whole sections.
seo.technicalVitalsD: Lighthouse's lab measurements — LCP, CLS and the rest — measured on the mobile profile Google indexes with. Green is good, red hurts ranking.
seo.linksBlurb: Every link on the page, checked for a live response. Broken links waste crawl budget and send visitors to dead ends.
seo.linksBrokenD: The target returned a 404 or didn't exist. Internal broken links are entirely in your control and should be fixed first.
seo.linksRedirectsD: The link resolves, but only after a hop. Each redirect costs a little crawl budget and load time — worth pointing links straight at the destination.
seo.linksErrorsD: The target server failed or was too slow to answer. Often temporary, so re-check before assuming it's dead.
seo.linksScopeD: Internal links point within your own site; external ones leave it. The scope column tells you which, so you know what you can fix directly.
seo.schemaBlurb: The structured data (JSON-LD) on the page — the machine-readable markup that powers rich results like ratings, FAQs and breadcrumbs.
seo.schemaBlocksD: Each JSON-LD block and the schema.org types it declares (Organization, Product, FAQPage…). More correct types mean more eligible rich results.
seo.schemaErrorsD: Markup that breaks the spec — a required property missing, or a wrong value type. These stop the rich result from showing at all.
seo.schemaRecommendedD: Optional properties that aren't required but make the rich result stronger, like an aggregateRating on a product or a search action on the site.
seo.crawlBlurb: A multi-page crawl of the site starting from this page, so you can see site-wide issues that a single-page audit can't — orphan pages, broken internal links, depth.
seo.crawlPagesD: How many pages the crawler reached by following internal links from the start URL. A low number can mean poor internal linking.
seo.crawlDepthD: How many clicks from the start page each page sits. Pages buried deep get crawled and ranked less often.
seo.crawlIssuesD: Problems found across the crawl — broken links, missing titles, noindex tags — aggregated so you can fix a pattern once.
seo.searchBlurb: Real search traffic for this site pulled from Search Console — the queries and pages actually bringing visitors in from Google.
seo.searchClicksD: Impressions are how often you appeared in results; clicks are how often someone chose you. The ratio is your click-through rate.
seo.searchQueriesD: The search terms sending you the most traffic. Terms with high impressions but few clicks are opportunities to improve the title or description.
seo.searchPositionD: Your average ranking for a query. Anything past the first page (position 10+) gets very little traffic no matter the impressions.
seo.compareBlurb: This page side by side with competitor URLs you add, so you can see where they're ahead on the on-page basics and close the gap.
seo.compareAddD: Paste a competing URL and we snapshot its meta, content and technical signals so the comparison is like-for-like.
seo.compareSideBySideD: Word count, title length, structured data and the rest, lined up in columns. A cell where they're green and you're not is a to-do.
seo.compareRefreshD: Competitor snapshots go stale as they change their pages. Refresh to re-fetch before you rely on the comparison.
seo.suggestionsBlurb: The specific performance opportunities Lighthouse found, worst first, each with what to change and roughly what it saves.
seo.suggestionsSortedD: The audits with the biggest score impact are at the top, so the first few entries are where your time pays back the most.
seo.suggestionsAdviceD: Plain-language guidance on the fix — defer this script, preload that font — plus the affected resources so you know where to look.
seo.suggestionsSavingD: Roughly how much load time or how many bytes the fix recovers. Use it to weigh effort against payback.
seo.historyBlurb: Every audit you've run for this site, newest first, so you can answer 'did that change actually help?'
seo.historyChangeD: The delta against the run before it. A green step up after a deploy is the proof a fix landed.
seo.historyOpenD: Click any row to load that older report back into the tabs — handy for seeing exactly what a page looked like before a change.
seo.historyBestD: The highest score recorded gets a marker, so you can tell at a glance whether you're improving or slipping back.
